bull_bear.body:
- National scale in cardiac care - single largest cardiac care provider in India, performing approximately 16% of all major heart surgeries nationwide
- Low-cost, high-volume affordable care model that has sustained pricing discipline over decades (e.g. still receives less than Rs 1.5 lakh for some sponsored heart patients)

- Provider-payer convergence - first Indian hospital group to secure a health insurance license (Narayana Health Insurance Limited) and to enable Health Savings Accounts with banking partners (Bank of Baroda, from 18 December 2025)

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Cybersecurity and data privacy — Flagged as the industry-wide top concern; NH is still moving towards full compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) and Rules thereunder, indicating compliance is not yet complete.
- Fire safety and emergency preparedness — Management explicitly cites recent media reports of serious fire incidents at multiple hospitals across the country, and the inherent difficulty of evacuating critical patients, as an industry-wide hazard requiring continued infrastructure investment.
- Global supply chain and vendor disruption — The Ukraine war and, more recently, the Iran conflict are cited as ongoing disruptors of global supply chains for life-saving and critical medical supplies; management states NH is 'not immune' to these impacts.
- Expansion and integration risk — The FY26 acquisition of 12 Practice Plus Group hospitals in the UK creates execution risk around integrating new facilities, cultural alignment and maintaining operational consistency as NH's global footprint grows.
- Foreign currency risk — NH has a structural mismatch between the currencies of sales, purchases and borrowings and its INR functional currency (USD/GBP exposure from Cayman and UK operations), requiring active hedging via forward contracts and interest rate swaps.
- Interest rate risk on variable-rate borrowings — The Company's main interest rate risk arises from long-term borrowings carrying variable rates, exposing it to cash-flow interest rate risk that management manages by balancing fixed vs floating rate instruments.
- Technology obsolescence — Medical and IT infrastructure, including robotic surgical equipment, requires continual reassessment and upgrade to avoid obsolescence and maintain competitive clinical capability.
- Workforce and talent management — Management identifies people (consultant doctors, nurses, medical support technicians) as its most important asset and a key risk area, requiring sustained investment in training, well-being and leadership development to mitigate attrition/availability risk.

- Global diversification through measured, disciplined geographic expansion (Cayman Islands, and UK via the Practice Plus Group acquisition) to access stable/mature markets, mitigate India concentration risk and enhance revenue resilience
- Disciplined, demand-linked domestic capacity creation - physical infrastructure treated as an outcome of strategy (clinical capability, digital integration, ecosystem synergies), not the driver of growth
- Scaling Narayana Aditi, a purpose-built health insurance product for India's underinsured 'missing middle', tightly integrating clinical care delivery with financial protection to build provider-payer convergence
- Technology as core infrastructure - advancing the Athma (patient/clinical/admin workflow) and Medha (analytics) platforms from efficiency tools into strategic assets, with a structured AI intelligence-maturity framework (foundational, actionable, agentic) and a unified data layer
- Embedding enterprise-wide clinical governance and accountability - institutionalised peer reviews/second opinions, continuous monitoring of procedure appropriateness and outcome variance, standardized clinical protocols
- Centralising and professionalising talent acquisition/HR (Talent Acquisition Shared Services model) with capability-led, selective hiring and continued investment in internal talent pipelines and leadership development
- Continuing investment in clinical research infrastructure (IRB/EC expansion, NH Bio-Bank, Narayana Clinical Research India Foundation) to sustain research output and academic recognition
- Sustained focus on 'Beyond Safe' / Zero Harm Healthcare as a continuing safety and quality discipline rather than a fixed target
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Narayana Health has embarked on a significant capital expenditure programme to enhance healthcare delivery capacity and build a foundation for future growth, with an initial outlay of approximately Rs 30,000 million already announced and additional investments currently under consideration. The current phase focuses on strengthening existing hubs with a substantial presence - Bangalore, Kolkata and Raipur - and targets growing total network bed capacity from 5,750 beds (as of 31 March 2026) to a pipeline target of 7,680 beds by FY30, via six named projects: (1) a 215-bed greenfield hospital at HSR, Bangalore, with the main contractor onboarded and the project progressing on schedule for FY28 completion; (2) a 350-bed greenfield hospital at Rajarhat, Kolkata, with sanctions in place and progressing on schedule for FY28 completion; (3) a 220-bed leased facility in Central Bangalore, with the lease and construction agreement executed and design/approvals in process, targeted for FY28; (4) a 350-bed greenfield hospital in South Bangalore, with design and approvals in process, targeted for FY29; (5) a 300-bed expansion of the existing Raipur hospital, with the main contractor onboarded and progressing on schedule for FY28 completion; and (6) a 100-bed leased facility in South-West Bangalore, with structural work completed and MEP/interior fit-out under way, targeted for FY27. Internationally, NH completed the acquisition (via its wholly-owned Cayman Islands subsidiary Health City Cayman Islands Ltd and its UK step-down subsidiary Narayana Hrudayalaya UK Ltd) of Practice Plus Group Hospitals Ltd in the United Kingdom, which runs 7 hospitals, 3 surgical centres, 2 urgent treatment centres, 3 musculoskeletal/diagnostic centres and 1 ophthalmology centre with 330-bed capacity. NH also incorporated Practice Plus Group Property Ltd (11 March 2026) as a UK Propco to acquire, hold, develop and maintain hospital real estate for exclusive captive use by its UK Opco hospital-operating entities, under an Opco/Propco structure. outlook.body:
- India's healthcare public spending remains structurally low (~Rs 1.06 lakh crore, ~2% of the Union Budget for FY27), which management frames as an opportunity for scalable, cost-efficient private-sector models to complement public provisioning
- India is described as entering a 'decisive execution phase' of healthcare evolution, transitioning from historical underinvestment toward more structured and sustained expansion
- Push toward universal health coverage under the Viksit Bharat 2047 vision is expected to unlock significant unmet healthcare demand, particularly among the underinsured and middle-income segments
- The 'missing middle' segment - too affluent for state support, insufficiently covered by private/employer insurance - is highlighted as a large underserved demand pool that products like Narayana Aditi target
- India's health insurance segment grew ~15% YoY to a record gross written premium of Rs 1.37 lakh crore in FY26, driven by retail health policy traction following the FY25 GST rate reduction and record persistency - seen as a tailwind for provider-payer integration

open.item: A comprehensive senior-citizen-specific insurance product is being worked on with an intended rollout sometime next year.
Cayman maintenance capex budgeted at INR 457 million for the year, of which ~INR 158 million incurred so far; major Cayman capital outlay is otherwise complete.
Overheads run at ~28% without UK and ~23% with UK included, since PPG comes in at a lower overhead structure than the group.
~100-bed Bangalore addition is progressing as planned and expected to be commissioned by Q1 (as stated 'FY26'; given the call is Q2 FY26 this most plausibly refers to Q1 FY27).

CGHS rate revision expected to give ~30% benefit on packages and up to ~12% on non-packaged components, translating to ~1% benefit on monthly revenues with 70-80% flowing to EBITDA; pure CGHS impact ~INR 2-2.5 crore/month (~INR 30-50 crore annualized including other PSU payers) once all come in line, likely by ~Q2 next year.

Cayman insurance ran ~USD 5 million quarterly loss at ~110-112% loss ratio on a ~USD 60 million annualized premium (ramped faster than expected); price increases kick in June for ~30-35% of accounts plus purging of unfavorably priced accounts, so losses should come down significantly over the next ~3 quarters (maybe 1-2 more quarters at this range).

Kolkata/Eastern cluster (26% revenue share) grew only ~5-6% due to the deliberate shift from international to domestic patients and case-mix prioritization; volume growth is expected to recover in the coming 2-3 quarters via digital marketing, clinics, insurance and clinical-team strengthening.

Clinics (11 in Bangalore) to expand further in Bangalore and enter Calcutta in FY27, with a plan to double the current clinic count (paced against property acquisition, rent and controlled cash losses); from FY27 the clinic business will be rolled into the hospital business reporting.

India business to grow at 'normal' (roughly high-single/low-double-digit) organic growth in line with market and internal efficiency efforts until the major capacity expansions come online in 2-3 years, when the next inflection point occurs.
Company intends to keep capex at a INR 1500-1600 crore run rate for the next 3 years, of which at least ~80% will be funded through debt, so leverage will increase.
Management historically targets a net-debt/EBITDA ceiling of ~2x but expects to run higher leverage over the next 2-3 years due to stepped-up capex, funded significantly through debt.
Greenfield/brownfield hospital projects in Bangalore and Kolkata will take a two-to-three-year build cycle before capex builds up on these units.

FY26 greenfield capex was only ~INR 109 crore vs ~INR 424 crore planned (~74% miss) due to election-related construction-labour and permission delays; the FY28 commissioning timeline for Rajarhat, HSR, Raipur and Bangalore still holds.

New hospitals commissioning in FY27/FY28 will have break-even characteristics in line with market and realizations at a discount to current market prices in those geographies; some margin impact expected, aiming to keep dilution/breakeven in line with peers.

Rajarhat (New Town Kolkata) greenfield: ~1000-bed project with ~INR 1000 crore capex in phases over ten years; construction to finish and first phase commence by FY28, with EBITDA break-even estimated between the 2nd and 3rd year.

~INR 3000 crore of projects announced, ~80% to be borrowed and repaid over 10-15 years; ~INR 2400 crore incremental debt to come on books over the next 3 years plus ~INR 300-350 crore annual regular capex, implying ~INR 800-1000 crore gross debt addition per year minus repayments.

India capex plan of ~INR 3000 crore over the next three years across greenfield, brownfield, O&M and acquisitions; FY27 capex guidance to be given closer to year-end, with project-by-project timelines in the investor deck.

Committed greenfield projects in Kolkata and Bangalore (~700 beds) plus Raipur brownfield (~150 beds), targeting close to ~1500 total beds added over the next four years, with the large portion in years 3 and 4.

Total announced project capex ~INR 3000 crore (of which greenfield organic ~INR 460 crore), all expected to be commissioned by FY28-FY29, implying roughly ~INR 1000 crore of capex in each of FY28 and FY29.

Management is comfortable with net-debt/EBITDA up to ~3x (internal discipline not to breach), likely reaching there by end of the 4th year if all planned projects proceed, after which it should fall rapidly as new hospitals turn EBITDA-positive.

Management explicitly cites recent media reports of serious fire incidents at multiple hospitals across the country, and the inherent difficulty of evacuating critical patients, as an industry-wide hazard requiring continued infrastructure investment.

risks.risk: Global supply chain and vendor disruption
risks.note: The Ukraine war and, more recently, the Iran conflict are cited as ongoing disruptors of global supply chains for life-saving and critical medical supplies; management states NH is 'not immune' to these impacts.

The FY26 acquisition of 12 Practice Plus Group hospitals in the UK creates execution risk around integrating new facilities, cultural alignment and maintaining operational consistency as NH's global footprint grows.

NH has a structural mismatch between the currencies of sales, purchases and borrowings and its INR functional currency (USD/GBP exposure from Cayman and UK operations), requiring active hedging via forward contracts and interest rate swaps.

risks.risk: Interest rate risk on variable-rate borrowings
risks.note: The Company's main interest rate risk arises from long-term borrowings carrying variable rates, exposing it to cash-flow interest rate risk that management manages by balancing fixed vs floating rate instruments.
Medical and IT infrastructure, including robotic surgical equipment, requires continual reassessment and upgrade to avoid obsolescence and maintain competitive clinical capability.

Management identifies people (consultant doctors, nurses, medical support technicians) as its most important asset and a key risk area, requiring sustained investment in training, well-being and leadership development to mitigate attrition/availability risk.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's healthcare public spending remains structurally low (~Rs 1.06 lakh crore, ~2% of the Union Budget for FY27), which management frames as an opportunity for scalable, cost-efficient private-sector models to complement public provisioning
- India is described as entering a 'decisive execution phase' of healthcare evolution, transitioning from historical underinvestment toward more structured and sustained expansion
- Push toward universal health coverage under the Viksit Bharat 2047 vision is expected to unlock significant unmet healthcare demand, particularly among the underinsured and middle-income segments
- The 'missing middle' segment - too affluent for state support, insufficiently covered by private/employer insurance - is highlighted as a large underserved demand pool that products like Narayana Aditi target
- India's health insurance segment grew ~15% YoY to a record gross written premium of Rs 1.37 lakh crore in FY26, driven by retail health policy traction following the FY25 GST rate reduction and record persistency - seen as a tailwind for provider-payer integration

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Narayana Health has embarked on a significant capital expenditure programme to enhance healthcare delivery capacity and build a foundation for future growth, with an initial outlay of approximately Rs 30,000 million already announced and additional investments currently under consideration. The current phase focuses on strengthening existing hubs with a substantial presence - Bangalore, Kolkata and Raipur - and targets growing total network bed capacity from 5,750 beds (as of 31 March 2026) to a pipeline target of 7,680 beds by FY30, via six named projects: (1) a 215-bed greenfield hospital at HSR, Bangalore, with the main contractor onboarded and the project progressing on schedule for FY28 completion; (2) a 350-bed greenfield hospital at Rajarhat, Kolkata, with sanctions in place and progressing on schedule for FY28 completion; (3) a 220-bed leased facility in Central Bangalore, with the lease and construction agreement executed and design/approvals in process, targeted for FY28; (4) a 350-bed greenfield hospital in South Bangalore, with design and approvals in process, targeted for FY29; (5) a 300-bed expansion of the existing Raipur hospital, with the main contractor onboarded and progressing on schedule for FY28 completion; and (6) a 100-bed leased facility in South-West Bangalore, with structural work completed and MEP/interior fit-out under way, targeted for FY27. Internationally, NH completed the acquisition (via its wholly-owned Cayman Islands subsidiary Health City Cayman Islands Ltd and its UK step-down subsidiary Narayana Hrudayalaya UK Ltd) of Practice Plus Group Hospitals Ltd in the United Kingdom, which runs 7 hospitals, 3 surgical centres, 2 urgent treatment centres, 3 musculoskeletal/diagnostic centres and 1 ophthalmology centre with 330-bed capacity. NH also incorporated Practice Plus Group Property Ltd (11 March 2026) as a UK Propco to acquire, hold, develop and maintain hospital real estate for exclusive captive use by its UK Opco hospital-operating entities, under an Opco/Propco structure. Domestically, NH Integrated Care's clinic network (11 points of presence: 10 clinics in Bengaluru, 1 in Hosur) has scaled since its FY24 inception, with revenue growing from Rs 418 million in FY25 to Rs 772 million in FY26.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- National scale in cardiac care - single largest cardiac care provider in India, performing approximately 16% of all major heart surgeries nationwide
- Low-cost, high-volume affordable care model that has sustained pricing discipline over decades (e.g. still receives less than Rs 1.5 lakh for some sponsored heart patients)
- Integration of standalone cardiac care with oncology and bone-marrow-transplant services at Health City Bangalore, giving it the highest number of BMTs in India, particularly for children
- Proprietary, in-house-built digital healthcare platforms (Athma - open-source hospital information management system, and Medha) developed over 10+ years, providing an integrated patient-doctor-nurse-technician-equipment digital architecture
- Provider-payer convergence - first Indian hospital group to secure a health insurance license (Narayana Health Insurance Limited) and to enable Health Savings Accounts with banking partners (Bank of Baroda, from 18 December 2025)
- Global leadership in robotic-assisted cardiac surgery - largest number of robotic-assisted cardiac surgeries in the world across its Da Vinci robotic units
- Tri-continental hospital operating footprint (Asia, Europe, Caribbean) - only Indian healthcare group with direct hospital ownership/management experience across all three regions
- Strong employer brand enabling talent pipeline leverage across group entities

The India revenue chart is on a materially smaller and differently defined base — the deck footnotes that its India total revenue is excluding ATHMA, Medha and adjusted with Inter Company eliminations — so the two should not be read as the same measure.
- [Deck hygiene] The presentation is filed as a "Revised Investor Presentation for the quarter ended June 30, 2026" dated August 03, 2026, but the cover page carries the stale date "August 02, 2023".

themes.need: Under-bedded India plus insurance penetration and preventive-care adoption drive a domestic healthcare capex + volume cycle distinct from export pharma. MAXHEALTH adding ~2,500+ beds (Gurgaon 500-bed by FY27); APOLLOHOSP/MEDANTA/KIMS/NH/ASTERDM/MAXHEALTH on hospitals; LALPATHLAB/METROPOLIS/THYROCARE/VIJAYA on diagnostics (LALPATHLAB guides 13-15% FY27); MEDPLUS/ENTERO on pharmacy/distribution; POLYMED on devices. The same India-only demand engine now also carries India-facing branded pharma, which is driven by domestic volume and price rather than the export book: GLAXO delivered its first INR 1,000cr quarter with 8.1% revenue growth, Shingrix at a ~INR 75cr annual run-rate (CY25, +80% YoY) and Jemperli's first-line approval expanding eligible patients from 800 to 6,000; ERIS (dermatology 15% of revenue after INR 1,265cr of domestic brand acquisitions), SANOFI (India-for-India, NLEM price cuts) and THEMISMED (hospital segment +20% YoY) sit on the same axis.
themes.driver: New-bed commissioning + occupancy ramp; Tier 3/4 diagnostics penetration; CGHS rate revision; preventive-test volumes; domestic branded-formulation volume growth and NLEM/price actions.
